title: Capstone Part 2: Build and Integrate
summary: With a solid plan from Part 1, Part 2 is where you construct the automation, applying the full range of skills from the previous weeks in a realistic, integrated build - this is the hands-on core of your capstone. You work from your design, building
content:
# Capstone Part 2: Build and Integrate ##### The gap between the diagram and the thing Your Part 1 plan is clean. Boxes, arrows, a data model, a risk table. Every arrow says something reasonable like "update order status." Then you build it, and the reality of arrow number three turns out to be: the supplier's email `Message-ID` header is missing on forwarded messages, so your deduplication key is null a third of the time; the date arrives as `14-03-26` which could be three things; and the API you planned to call returns `200 OK` with `{"error": "not found"}` in the body rather than a 404. None of this means the plan was wrong. **Every plan meets reality at integration time**, and handling that gap well is the actual craft. Today you build — applying six weeks of skills to one real system — and the most important thing you produce is not the workflow but the discipline of how you build it. ##### Build in vertical slices, not layers The instinct is to build left to right: get the trigger working, then step two, then step three. This is slower than it looks, because you do not discover that step seven's API rejects your data format until day three. Build **vertical slices** instead: get one record all the way through the simplest possible path first, then add branches, transformation quality and error handling. ```text SLICE 1 (today's practical task) trigger → parse → write to DB → done One happy-path record, end to end. Proves the plumbing. SLICE 2 add the second integration and real data mapping SLICE 3 add branching (the discrepancy path) SLICE 4 add the AI step + validation SLICE 5 add error handling, retries, dead-letter SLICE 6 add logging, alerts, monitoring ``` Each slice is independently testable and independently demonstrable. If you run out of time, you have something that works rather than six half-built layers. ##### Integrating and authenticating each system Work through one system at a time, and follow the same sequence every time: 1. **Read the API docs first** — auth method, the exact endpoint, required fields, rate limits, pagination, and the error format. 2. **Test outside the workflow.** Use `curl` or Postman with real credentials. When something fails here, you know it is the API and not your mapping — this one habit saves hours. 3. **Store the credential properly** in the platform's credential manager, named descriptively, scoped minimally. 4. **Make the simplest possible call** inside the workflow. 5. **Inspect the actual response** in the node's output panel. Not the documented response — the actual one. They differ more often than you would like. 6. **Then** map the real fields. ```bash # Step 2 in practice — prove the integration works before wiring it up curl -X PATCH "https://api.supplierportal.com/v2/purchase-orders/PO-4471" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPPLIER_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"confirmed_date":"2026-03-20","confirmed_qty":120}' \ -w "\nHTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n" ``` Keep an **integration log** as you go — a short table of system, auth method, endpoint, quirks discovered, and rate limits. It becomes part of your documentation tomorrow, and writing it while the pain is fresh is far easier than reconstructing it later. ##### Implementing transformation and logic This is where Day 17's material earns its place. Build the transformation as one explicit, named step rather than scattering conversions across a dozen mapped fields. ```javascript // n8n Code node: "Normalize supplier confirmation" // Input : raw parsed email fields (all strings, all untrusted) // Output: a typed, validated record ready for the database const out = []; for (const item of $input.all()) { const r = item.json; // --- PO number: uppercase, strip stray characters --- const po = String(r.po_number ?? '').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z0-9\-]/g, ''); // --- Date: accept DD-MM-YY / DD-MM-YYYY / DD/MM/YYYY -> ISO --- const m = String(r.confirmed_date ?? '').match(/^(\d{1,2})[-/](\d{1,2})[-/](\d{2,4})$/); let isoDate = null; if (m) { const [, d, mo, y] = m; const year = y.length === 2 ? `20${y}` : y; isoDate = `${year}-${mo.padStart(2, '0')}-${d.padStart(2, '0')}`; } // --- Numbers: strip separators and currency symbols --- const qty = parseInt(String(r.qty ?? '').replace(/[^\d]/g, ''), 10); const price = Number(String(r.price ?? '').replace(/[^0-9.]/g, '')); const valid = Boolean(po) && Boolean(isoDate) && Number.isFinite(qty) && qty > 0 && Number.isFinite(price) && price >= 0; out.push({ json: { po_number: po || null, confirmed_date: isoDate, confirmed_qty: Number.isFinite(qty) ? qty : null, confirmed_price: Number.isFinite(price) ? price : null, source_message_id: r.message_id ?? null, valid, invalid_reason: valid ? null : [!po && 'missing PO', !isoDate && 'unparseable date', !Number.isFinite(qty) && 'bad quantity'].filter(Boolean).join('; '), }, }); } return out; ``` Two habits embedded there worth copying into everything you build: **every field has a fallback** so one missing value cannot crash the run, and the record carries its own **validity verdict with a reason**, so a downstream filter can route bad records to a human with an explanation attached. The business logic then reads cleanly, because the data is already clean: ```sql -- Idempotent state update: safe to run twice on the same email INSERT INTO processed_emails (message_id, po_number) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING message_id; -- If this returns no row, the email was already handled → stop the branch. ``` ##### Adding error handling and security Apply Day 18 and Day 30 as you build, not afterwards. Retrofitting error handling into a finished workflow is far more work than including it in each slice. The build checklist: - **Dedup at the entry point** — a unique key on an event or message ID. - **Validate before acting** — required fields, types, ranges; route failures to a review queue rather than crashing. - **Retry transient failures** (429, 5xx, timeouts) with exponential backoff, capped at 3–5 attempts. - **Dead-letter permanent failures** — write the record and error to a `failed_items` table so nothing vanishes. - **Alert on failure** with context, deduplicated, on the error path (not after the failing step). - **Idempotent writes** — upserts, not blind inserts, so a re-run is always safe. - **Credentials in the credential store**, scoped minimally, never in node parameters. - **Webhook signature verification** on every inbound webhook. - **Redact PII and secrets** from logs. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Trigger] --> B[Verify signature] B --> C{Dedup: seen this ID?} C -->|yes| Z[Stop — duplicate] C -->|no| D[Normalize + validate] D -->|invalid| R[Review queue
+ reason + Slack notice] D -->|valid| E[Main integration
retry 3x, backoff] E -->|transient failure| Q[Dead-letter table
+ high alert] E -->|success| F[Update state — upsert] F --> G[Notify / digest] G --> H[Log run outcome] R --> H Q --> H ``` ##### Iterating with test data Build a **test fixture set** early — a folder of realistic sample payloads you can replay at will. This is the single biggest productivity investment in the build phase, because it turns "wait for a real email to arrive" into "click Execute." ```text _fixtures/ ├── 01-happy-path.json complete, well-formed ├── 02-missing-po.json required field absent ├── 03-weird-date.json "14-03-26" ├── 04-price-with-symbol.json "₹1,299.00" ├── 05-duplicate.json same message_id as 01 ├── 06-quantity-mismatch.json triggers the discrepancy branch ├── 07-unknown-po.json PO not in the database └── 08-empty-body.json nothing parseable ``` Then iterate tightly: run one fixture, inspect every node's input and output, fix one thing, re-run. Use single-node execution (n8n's per-node play button, Make's *Run this module only*) so you are not re-running the whole workflow to test step six. Keep a **build log** as you go — a running note of what you tried, what failed, and what fixed it. Tomorrow's documentation and today's assignment both come almost free from it. ##### Common pitfalls - **Building left to right** instead of in vertical slices. - **Testing only with your own perfect data.** - **Skipping the curl test** and debugging mapping when the problem is authentication. - **Deferring error handling** to "after it works." - **Hard-coding an ID or URL** during testing and forgetting to parameterize it. - **Not saving progress** — export the workflow to Git at the end of every slice. - **Ignoring rate limits** while testing in a loop and getting your key throttled. - **Changing several things at once** when debugging. - **Building against production data** — use test credentials and a test database. - **Scope creep mid-build.** Write new ideas on a phase-2 list and keep going. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is slice one and two: implement the **trigger and at least the first two integrations end to end on test data**, with authentication, data mapping, and a first pass of error handling. Resist the urge to make it complete — make it *work*, then extend. The mini project is the **full capstone build**: all systems integrated, logic and transformations implemented, a **database for state and deduplication**, **error handling and security** applied, and the whole workflow verified against your **normal and edge-case fixtures**. Run every fixture and record the outcome in a table; that table is a large part of tomorrow's documentation and it is exactly the artefact from Day 29's test-plan discipline. For the assignment, **document your build process** including **one significant integration problem** — what happened, how you diagnosed it, and how you solved it. Be specific and technical: "the webhook payload arrived form-encoded rather than JSON, so every field mapped to null; I confirmed it by inspecting the raw body in webhook.site, then set the Content-Type on the sender." That paragraph is worth more in an interview than a list of tools, because debugging stories are how experienced engineers recognize each other. ##### Key takeaways - Build in vertical slices — one record end to end first, then branches, quality and reliability — so you always have something that works. - Integrate one system at a time: read the docs, prove it with curl, store the credential properly, then map real fields from the *actual* response. - Put transformation in one explicit step with fallbacks for every field and a validity verdict that carries its own reason. - Add dedup, validation, retries, dead-lettering, alerts and idempotent writes as you build each slice, not afterwards. - Create a fixture set of normal and edge-case payloads early, iterate with single-node execution, and keep a build log that becomes your documentation.
